# ADR-13. The context pack is committed, generated by hand, and checked in CI

Closes PLAN-6. The contract is `docs/specs/context-pack.md`, which was written
before the generator and amended twice on the day this was accepted; this ADR
records the decisions the spec now carries and, as PLAN-6 asks, what the pack
leaves out.

The pack is a versioned description of this warehouse that lets a capable LLM
query it correctly and tells it what to refuse. Two files per target under
`context-pack/`: the JSON is the artifact and the markdown is a rendering of it
for direct prompt injection, carrying strictly less. Both are committed, which
makes them the only generated files in this repo that are.

## Context

Three constraints decided this, and none of them is a preference.

**The artifact is generated, committed, and therefore able to rot silently.**
Every other generated thing here is gitignored, so a stale one is a local
annoyance. A committed pack that no longer describes the warehouse is a
document that reads complete and is wrong, which is the exact failure the
refusal list exists to prevent a consumer from causing.

**ADR-1 keeps CI credential-free, so the only warehouse a pull request can
build is the fixture one.** `make ci-build` runs the whole pipeline from
committed JSON fixtures. That warehouse has the right shape and seven-row
tables. A pack generated there would carry fixture row counts, fixture profiles
and fixture example results, and committing it would make the artifact describe
something no consumer will ever read.

**The markdown is what gets used, and it is budgeted.** The JSON is about 9,000
lines; nothing puts it in a prompt. So a block that is in the JSON and not in
the markdown is, in practice, a block a model does not see, and every rendering
decision is a decision about what reaches the answering model. Everything
present is 25,219 estimated tokens against a budget of 26,000.

## Options considered

### Which warehouse the check runs against

**A. CI regenerates the pack and fails on a diff.** The strongest gate
available: the artifact could never be stale. Two things kill it. The numbers
would be the fixture zone's, per the constraint above. And generation is not
deterministic even against an unchanged warehouse: `generated_at`, the dbt
`invocation_id`, the manifest timestamp and the clock-derived columns of
`mart_pipeline_freshness` all move on a re-run with no data having moved.
Measured 2026-08-07: regenerating against an untouched warehouse produced a
40-line diff, every line of it a clock. `git diff --exit-code` would fire on
every pull request, which is a gate someone switches off in a week.

**B. No CI gate. A pre-commit hook on a machine with the real zone.** Honest
about who can regenerate. It fails as a gate for the reason it is proposed: it
runs only where someone already has the warehouse and already knows, it cannot
run on a fresh clone or a fork at all, and pre-commit hooks that error on a
machine with no `data/sf.duckdb` get skipped with `--no-verify` and then
forgotten.

**C. CI checks the committed pack against the fixture warehouse, and generates
nothing.** Chosen. It rests on one property, which was measured rather than
assumed.

`--check` compares exactly four things: the target name, the `prose_revision`,
the `spec_version` and the per-model schema hash. The first three are file
reads and are as true on a runner as anywhere. The fourth is the only one that
needs a warehouse, and `publish/export.py`'s hash is over column names, types
and ordinal position, none of which depend on how many rows a fixture holds.
**Measured 2026-08-07: all 19 schema hashes computed from the fixture warehouse
are identical to the ones the real warehouse produced.** Both failure modes
were then demonstrated against that warehouse rather than argued: a moved
schema hash and a moved spec version each exit 3.

Row counts, profiles, freshness and example results are the only parts a
fixture zone gets wrong, and none of them is compared. That is the whole of why
this works, and it is also the limit: this gate cannot tell that the pack's
numbers are a month old.

### Whether the traps block belongs in the compact markdown

**A. JSON only.** The reading PLAN-6 step 2 shipped: section 9's rendering
order did not list traps, the markdown is allowed to carry less, and a trap
does not make a question unanswerable, so a prompt-sized rendering can do
without it. Defensible, and it was not obviously deliberate.

**B. Rendered, and droppable under budget pressure.** Puts traps in the ladder
beside profile statistics.

**C. Rendered, and never dropped.** Chosen, and the spec was amended to say so.
Two arguments, and the first is the one that settles it. **A trap is an
unconditional disclosure**: section 4.6 defines it as a disclosure object
without the trigger condition, so rendering the conditional warning and
withholding the unconditional one is the wrong way round. Second, three of the
four traps prevent a query that returns a plausible number rather than an
error: a `group by category` that pools three unrelated vocabularies, an H3
cell compared as a hexadecimal string, and an inner join that silently discards
the rows where `analysis_neighborhood` is null. What a trap changes is the
query that gets written, and it cannot change it from a file nobody reads.

B loses on arithmetic. The traps are 585 estimated tokens against a models
block of about 16,000. A rendering that has dropped every profile statistic and
kept every trap is the right shape for a prompt; the reverse is not, and the
ladder exists to shed detail from the models block rather than to choose
between kinds of prose.

## Decision

**The pack format.** One pack per target, named in its identity block, two
files, JSON authoritative. Three targets, one generator, one hand-maintained
prose file, `prose.yml`, whose hash every pack carries as `prose_revision` so a
consumer holding two packs can tell whether they came from one source. Nothing
derivable from the dbt manifest, the catalog, the registry or the published
manifest may appear in the prose. Section 3 of the spec fixes the top-level
keys and is the contract; this ADR does not restate it.

**Generation is by hand, after `make build`, on a machine with the real zone.**
`make context-pack`. Not in CI, not in a hook, not on a schedule.

**CI checks and never generates.** One step in the `dbt-duckdb` job, after
`dbt build`, running `--check` against the fixture warehouse. It fails the pull
request on a moved schema hash, a moved prose revision, a moved spec version or
a model set that has changed. Regenerating from fixtures to make it green is
the one wrong answer, and the workflow comment says so at the point of use.

**Four things fail generation**, unchanged from PLAN-6 step 3 and restated here
because softening one is how this artifact would decay: a model with no grain
sentence, a prose entry claiming a target while citing something that target
does not have, an example query that errors or whose SQL no longer matches the
hash a human attested to, and a rendering that cannot fit the budget with every
refusal, disclosure, trap and grain sentence present.

**The markdown carries the traps block**, rendered after the disclosures and
before the schema, and never dropped.

## What the pack leaves out

PLAN-6 asks the closing ADR to record this specifically. Spec section 10 is the
first six; the rest are the departures PLAN-6 step 2 recorded, now settled.

- **No consumer, and no measurement of whether models honour the refusals.**
  The refusal format is designed against how models fail, not measured against
  it. PLAN-6 puts every reader of the pack out of scope, on the ground that
  building the artifact and building something that reads it at once means
  neither constrains the other honestly. This is the largest omission and it is
  deliberate.
- **No arrival-lag measurement.** `refuse.newest-month-is-partial` is the one
  entry that warns without a number, and it says so. Deriving it needs row
  counts by month across two builds, which nothing here stores.
- **No per-dataset licence.** One statement covers the pack, the one
  `publish/export.py` already writes, although DataSF and the Census are
  different publishers under the same public-domain terms.
- **No semantic layer, no metric definitions, no natural-language-to-SQL
  grammar.** A metrics layer is a different artifact and would need its own
  decision.
- **No cross-target diff.** Three packs can disagree; `prose_revision` makes
  that detectable and nothing reconciles it.
- **The `bigquery` pack is not built in CI**, has no schema hash, and will be
  stale more often than not. `publish/export.py` renders DuckDB type names, so
  every hash would differ for a schema that is identical; the pack states the
  absence with its reason and names `make parity-columns` as the guarantee in
  its place. An absent field with a reason is a fact, an omitted one is a bug
  waiting to be reported.
- **Two of the three packs do not exist yet.** Only `duckdb` is generated.
  `published` and `bigquery` are declared in `pack_target.py` with their model
  sets, freshness sources and schema-hash policies, so `applies_to: [published]`
  in the prose is already meaningful and already validated; `open_target` raises
  for both rather than emitting a DuckDB pack under another name. What each
  needs is a connection factory and its own prose entries.
- **The join map is half derived.** dbt's `relationships` tests declare seven of
  the thirteen joins, so those are read from the manifest and the prose carries
  only the six no test declares, the dirty ones included. A prose join that
  restates a derived one fails generation.
- **The newest complete month comes from the data and not the clock.** It is the
  month before the month a column's maximum falls in. Reading it off today's
  date would move the pack at midnight on the first of the month with no data
  having moved, and turn the drift gate into a monthly false alarm.
- **Undocumented columns are reported and not fixed.** 178 warnings on the
  current run, almost all on staging models. The generator names each one and
  the markdown marks it `(no description in the yml)`, which is a real signal
  under the closed-world rule. That list is a to-do for the yml.

## Consequences

**Buys.** A model change that moves a column now fails the pull request that
makes it, on a runner, with no credentials and no bucket. The two things most
likely to rot, the prose and the contract, are compared by file hash and cannot
drift at all. And the pack is a diff: a reviewer sees the refusal that changed
next to the model that changed it.

**Costs.** The gate cannot see stale numbers. A pack whose row counts and
profiles are a month old passes every check, because the alternative is a gate
that fires on every ingest. Regeneration is a human step that can be forgotten,
and the only thing that catches a forgotten one is a schema change happening to
follow it. Amending the spec now invalidates every committed pack until someone
regenerates, which is the mechanism working and is still a chore. And the pack
is 25,219 tokens of committed artifact that a reviewer will not read line by
line.

**Lock-in.** The schema hash is `publish/export.py`'s, imported and not
reimplemented, so the pack inherits its DuckDB type rendering and the BigQuery
pack can never have one. The prose file is one file for three targets: it keeps
the copies honest and it means a published-only refusal still lands in the file
every other pack reads. Committing a generated artifact means every model change
carries a pack diff, which will be the largest hunk in some pull requests that
have nothing to do with the pack.

## Revisit if

- **A consumer appears.** The refusal format is designed against how models
  fail and has never been measured against one. The first evaluation is the
  point at which this whole format is worth arguing about with evidence rather
  than with reasoning.
- **The fixture check fails on a model nobody changed.** That means a model's
  shape depends on its data, which is a real defect and not a false alarm: no
  pack can describe such a model honestly for any warehouse but the one it was
  generated from. Fix the model rather than the gate.
- **The `published` pack lands and the three-pack argument does not survive it.**
  A second pack is the first real test of whether one prose file with
  `applies_to` beats three hand-kept documents.
- **The markdown stops fitting.** 25,219 against 26,000 leaves room for about
  one more mart. The budget is a canary and raising it is a decision, not a
  flag: the ladder already drops everything droppable before the failure.
